question: The EUROPOP2025 projections published by Eurostat predict that, between 2025 and 2100, the European Union will experience a natural demographic deficit of around 156.7 million people, offset in part by cumulative net migration of 103.7 million. Alternative scenarios also indicate that the model incorporates a ‘replacement migration’ mechanism designed to offset part of the decline in the working-age population.

At the same time, Eurostat emphasises that this immigration neither halts the ageing of the population nor provides a sustainable solution to the demographic imbalance1. Can the Commission clarify: 1.
whether it considers that increased reliance on non-European immigration constitutes a long-term policy objective to offset the Union’s demographic decline?
which studies demonstrate that this strategy would be more effective than an ambitious policy to support birth rates and labour market participation among European citizens?
Eurostat, ‘Population projections in the EU’, EUROPOP2025, 16 April 2025.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.11.2026) The EU supports Member States in their efforts to address the impacts of demographic change. The Commission’s 2023 Demography Toolbox1 is a structured framework for Member States, which mainstreams demographic considerations across EU policies; which is informed, but not driven by, statistical projections.

The Toolbox has four pillars – supporting parents, empowering young generations, sustaining the welfare of older generations and addressing labour shortages through managed legal migration where necessary, in full complementarity to harnessing talents from within the EU.

The proposal for the Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-2034 includes several options for Member States to address demographic challenges, notably through the National and Regional Partnership Plans, and the Commission is ready to support Member States in designing and implementing policies in this respect.

Evidence, including the report ‘Demographic transformation in the EU’2, demonstrates that migration can help address labour shortages and support growth, but cannot reverse population ageing or natural demographic decline. Migration is only one part of a broader European approach to demographic challenges.

At the same time, the Commission is supporting labour market activation, notably by targeting underrepresented groups; investing in skills, helping the young to transition from education to work; investing in childcare and care; prolonging working lives and increasing productivity.
Finally, analyses3 suggest that while family support measures can influence fertility levels and timing, the effects are typically modest and unlikely to return fertility to replacement rates4.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:52023DC0577. 2 https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147518. 3 https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC147518. 4 Replacement rates are the average number of children per woman required for a population to replace itself

across generations without immigration. Fertility levels in EU countries have been low for half a century, below the level of 2.1 children per woman that is generally needed to maintain a stable population, and are projected to remain low in the future (for further information, please see the following publication: https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/handle/JRC137492).
